Period I · 1618 → 15. Juli 1726 · Establishment under Danish and Gottorp rule
Holstein divided in two: the royal Danish part (Glückstadt, Pinneberg, Rantzau) and the Gottorp part (Tönning, Schleswig, Kiel) · no unified coinage structure · a premium between Species and circulating coins is the norm.
Dominant large silver coin: the Thaler Species in the 9¼-Fuß, established by Danish tradition; alongside it, Schilling petty coinage in Lübeck reckoning. Contemporary nomenclature: on the coins themselves «SPECIES» or a Mark-Danske denomination; auction catalogues often use «Speciedaler».
Main circulation in Holstein: besides domestic issues, Lübeck, Hamburg and North-German Thaler Species circulate; Dutch Patagonen/Albertusthaler; Swedish 4-Mark pieces; Spanish piastres — trade accepts every Species by silver content.
In parallel with the Thaler Species issues — the Kronemønt category (1618 → 1696). See the dedicated section 10½-Krone-Fuß · Kronemønt tariff coin below, which documents the tariff history 1½ → 1⅓ → ⅔ Speciedaler and the strike table 1644–1696 in detail.
Tönning mint · Gottorp Holstein · 1689–1726 · petty coins denominated in Lübeck reckoning (within the 9¼-Fuß system) plus Thaler Species and ducats (from the Bruun Coll., Stack's Bowers auction, Zurich 14–15 March 2025)
✦ Kurant coins — Full-value coinage Full-value · face value ≈ silver content · issued by the state without or with minor premium

 115.57363 101.12693 ? Kopenhagen 4 Speciedaler 1624 · Christian IV, Copenhagen, mintmaster Nicolaus Schwabe (clover privy mark, NS) · Davenport EC II 3521. CoinVarieties documents the specification as 115 g.888 at 43.7 mm diameter; the coin was «struck with regular Speciedaler dies but four times as thick». Christian IV recorded on 31 March receiving 140 Speciedalers from Schwabe struck from Norwegian silver — the 1624 series (1-, 2-, 3- and 4-Speciedaler) is the first Danish-Norwegian issue from Kongsberg silver (works established summer 1623). Bruun specimen 5364, — weighed 116.49 g.  9.63113 8.42724 ? Kopenhagen Obverse: monogram, reverse inscription ‹JUSTUS JEHOVA JUDEX›. Reduced to 14 Skilling by the Forordning of 21 March 1648. The inscription ‹JUSTUS JEHOVA JUDEX› (The Lord is a righteous judge) alludes to Christian 4's anger at the Swedish army's invasion and ravaging of Jutland in 1643-44. The coins struck on this occasion are called Ulfeldtmønter or Hebræere. The coin bears the fire-hook, mintmaster Heinrich Köhler's mark; the dies were cut by Hans zum Busch. A total of 37,019 daler were struck. danskmoent.dk (Hede c4h149)KMM 157985 (Inv. FP 1466.47)KMM 157986 (Inv. FP 1466.46)KMM 157987 (Inv. FP 1466.45)KMM 157989 (Inv. FP 1466.43)KMM 157995 (Inv.  19.26227 16.85449 32 Kopenhagen Copenhagen pendant to km-32 (Glückstadt Hebræermønt 1645) — same Tetragrammaton יהוה on the reverse, same reduced fineness .593 under the strain of the Torstensson War (1643–1645). Both mints — Copenhagen and Glückstadt — struck the Hebræermønt in parallel; Krause lists them as separate types (cf. KM# 32 for the Glückstadt parallel). Structurally identical to km-32: tariff unchanged at ⅓ Speciedaler, cumulative seigniorage premium from the debasement at about +27.6 %.
